text:
Interviewer: This is a United States Holocaust Memorial Museum interview with Mr. edg — Pete Miller, on May 16th, 2014, in Washington, D.C. Thank you very much, Mr. Miller, for agreeing to speak with us today.
Interviewee: You’re welcome.
Interviewer: We’re going to begin the interview at the very beginning. So, I’m going to ask a few questions about your childhood, about your family, about the town you were born in, or the village you were born in. So I’ll start now. Can you tell me please, your name at birth, your date of birth, and we’ll go from there.
Interviewee: My name is Pete Miller. Was born in 1931.
Interviewer: What was the date?
Interviewee: February 25th, 1931.
Interviewer: And was your name Miller also, when you were born?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Okay. Where were you born, Mr. Miller?
Interviewee: A li — a little town, was Poland that time. The name is Mlynov.
Interviewer: Mlynov. And —
Interviewee: To-Today they call it Mylniv, it’s Ukraine today.
Interviewer: Oh, so you were born in the —
Interviewee: Poland.
Interviewer: In Poland, but in the eastern section.
Interviewee: In the w — in the west.
Interviewer: In the west?
Interviewee: The west section, not the eastern.
Interviewer: Oh, I — but how could it b-border the Ukraine?
Interviewee: Til ’39, was Poland.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: In ’39, the Russian captured the west part of Ukraine, in what’s today called —
Interviewer: Yes, west part —
Interviewee: — west part —
Interviewer: — of Ukraine, that’s true.
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Okay, okay. And Mlynov, was it a large town?
Interviewee: A little town with about 1200 Jews living, and a couple hundred Gentiles: Ukrainian, Poles, Czechs some. And around was still villages.
Interviewer: So, it was small.
Interviewee: Small, very small town.
Interviewer: And most — but mostly, from you say, it was mostly a Jewish town.
Interviewee: I would say yes. The majority was Jewish.
Interviewer: What were your father and mother’s names?
Interviewee: My father’s name was Hans.
Interviewer: Hans.
Interviewee: Yes. And my mother’s name was Emma.
Interviewer: Emma. Do you remember her maiden name?
Interviewee: Yes. My mother’s name was Mash.
Interviewer: Mash.
Interviewee: And my father Miller.
Interviewer: Yeah. And were they also from Mlynov?
Interviewee: Yes. They — in there, yeah, yeah.
Interviewer: Okay. So did you have a larger family, aunts and uncles, and —
Interviewee: Yes, from both sides.
Interviewer: Yeah?
Interviewee: I would say about 200 people.
Interviewer: So your father’s side, do — did he have brothers and sisters?
Interviewee: I had one brother — two brothers and a sister.
Interviewer: You?
Interviewee: There were four kids, yes.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: I was the youngest one.
Interviewer: What are — what were their names?
Interviewee: My brother after me was Josef, and my sister, her name was a Jawa.
Interviewer: Jawa?
Interviewee: Yes. And my older brother, the oldest, was Jacheal.
Interviewer: Jachear?
Interviewee: Jacheal.
Interviewer: Jacheal.
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Mm-hm. And how much older was your oldest brother?
Interviewee: My oldest brother was eight years older than I am.
Interviewer: So he was born in 1923?
Interviewee: He was in 1922.
Interviewer: ’22.
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: In 1922. And how did your father support the family?
Interviewee: My father had a butcher shop, and he used to like be a middle man, selling cattle, buying cattle.
Interviewer: Would he go out to the villagers and buy cattle from them, or they would bring it to him?
Interviewee: In Mlynov was with the biggest market in the Wołyń area. Wołyń was like a county here.
Interviewer: Yeah.
Interviewee: The biggest market. Every Tuesday was a big market, from everything from A to Z.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: And he knows a lot of — or used to deal with a lot of farmers, a lot of *** and used to make a nice living.
Interviewer: And so, can you describe a little bit about how he would purchase the animals? Would he go out to the farms? Would they bring them — he was a kosher butcher, I take it?
Interviewee: Yeah. He knew a lot — all the villagers around there, you know.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: He was born there, he used to deal with them, handle with them, lend them some money, or — a lot of business did with them. He was a successful businessman.
Interviewer: What kind of a personality did he have?
Interviewee: He?
Interviewer: Yeah.
Interviewee: He was a sm-smart guy. He knew how to deal with people, with a lot of farmers, a lot of Czechs, Poles. He had a mix, it was a mixed ter — the majority was Ukrainian, but a lot of Poles, Czechs, villagers.
Interviewer: So, he must have spoken many languages.
Interviewee: He spoke Russian, he spoke Ukrainian, he spoke Polish, Jewish.
Interviewer: And at home? What did you all speak at home?
Interviewee: At home we used to speak Jewish.
Interviewer: So, Yiddish, yes?
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: Yiddish, okay. And, was he alone in this business?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: So, no help from the family, or did your mother help him sometimes?
Interviewee: My brother got older, used to help him here and there. But we were little.
Interviewer: Yeah, yeah, yeah. And did your father have brothers and sisters? Did you have aunts and uncles?
Interviewee: Yes, my — my father had three brothers and a sister.
Interviewer: And did you know them well?
Interviewee: Hm?
Interviewer: Did you know them well?
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: They lived in the area. And what were their businesses? What were wa — how did they make their livings?
Interviewee: One brother had a — a store of, you know, like a little supermarket, you know. The other one, I don’t remember. I don’t — I was — the war broke out in ’39.
Interviewer: You were young.
Interviewee: I was nine years old.
Interviewer: What are some of your earliest memories from childhood?
Interviewee: Hm?
Interviewer: What are some of your earliest memories from childhood?
Interviewee: I think I remember since I was fi — four or five years, when I went to cheder, you know.
Interviewer: Mm-hm. Tell us a little about that.
Interviewee: Huh?
Interviewer: Tell us a little about that.
Interviewee: In my town, I would say every child went to cheder. Then I — I got a Hebrew teacher. We were five, six kids, and he used to teach us. And then when they broke out the war, everything is gone.
Interviewer: Yeah. Well —
Interviewee: Then I went to school, to Polish school for two years.
Interviewer: You did?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Okay. So it was a public school?
Interviewee: Public school, yes.
Interviewer: And was this — were most of your friends in that school also Jewish, because the town was Jewish?
Interviewee: No, mixed.
Interviewer: Mixed.
Interviewee: Was mixed.
Interviewer: Okay. Did you ever experience prejudice in the — in the classroom?
Interviewee: We used to fight, but I don’t know if it was because I’m Jewish or not Jewish. Just kids, you know?
Interviewer: Yeah. And did you speak Polish, of course, in this —
Interviewee: Hm?
Interviewer: Did you speak Polish?
Interviewee: Yeah. Still remem — can si — communicate good.
Interviewer: Yeah? Okay. Tell us a little bit about your mother. What kind of a person was she?
Interviewee: About my mother?
Interviewer: Mm-hm.
Interviewee: My mother died, I think, in ’37.
Interviewer: Oh, so you were little.
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: You were little. Do you have memories of her?
Interviewee: Very little.
Interviewer: Yeah. As the youngest, you must have missed her very much.
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Yeah. Your brothers and sisters, since you were the youngest, was there someone who paid particular attention to you and helped you?
Interviewee: Yeah, next door my grandmother lived —
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: — with my mother’s — her sister. They used to take care of me.
Interviewer: And what do you remember about your grandmother? What kind of a person was she?
Interviewee: I remember almost everything. The names, the —
Interviewer: Tell me.
Interviewee: — where they lived. They used to come each to other, because the town was a little town, five houses, or six houses here there, the left to the right, th-they lived. There were also some of them had kids, my mother’s sister had two daughters. Another one had — my mother had three sisters, and three brothers also, there were seven kids.
Interviewer: Your — what was your grandmother’s name?
Interviewee: Hannah.
Interviewer: Hannah. And she was your mother’s mother?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Okay. Did you also know your father’s parents?
Interviewee: Only the grandmother.
Interviewer: Only the grandmother, okay.
Interviewee: Both died before I think I was born. One gr — one from — my mother’s father wasn’t — lived in United States for eight years.
Interviewer: Did he?
Interviewee: He came here in — after the war, 1920 or ’21, with some relatives, they live in Baltimore. And after eight years he came back, and a year or two he died, I think. Was before 1930.
